prohibited_recommendations: Do not start corticosteroids as monotherapy in suspected GBS.
Do not assume MG and start anticholinesterase / steroid therapy without supportive serology / EMG when areflexia is present.
required_recommendations: Obtain anti-GQ1b and broader ganglioside panel.
Bedside ice-pack test and AChR antibody assay to evaluate MG.
RNS or single-fibre EMG if MG remains a serious consideration.
Initiate IVIG / plasma exchange if GBS variant confirmed.
Brainstem MRI to exclude structural cause.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome, cranial variant — isolated bilateral ptosis with global areflexia

differential.key_features: Bilateral ptosis is the cardinal MG sign; preserved reflexes and fatigability favour MG. Ice-pack test, AChR antibodies, and RNS / single-fibre EMG distinguish.
Areflexia is shared; absence of ophthalmoplegia and ataxia argues against classic MFS; anti-GQ1b panel helpful.
Proximal weakness and autonomic features dominate; reflexes augment with effort; RNS shows incremental response.
Chronic course over years, not acute days; preserved reflexes.
Bilateral isolated ptosis without other brainstem findings is rare in stroke; MRI excludes.

key_clinical_evidence: Global areflexia in a patient with isolated ptosis is the discriminating sign — MG preserves reflexes.
Albuminocytologic dissociation and demyelinating EMG features support GBS cranial variant.
Anti-GQ1b and anti-GT1a panel positive in many MFS-spectrum cranial variants.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Global areflexia, elevated CSF protein, and demyelinating EMG indicate a GBS cranial variant rather than MG.
red_herrings.data_point: Isolated bilateral ptosis without ophthalmoplegia or weakness
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on myasthenia gravis as the textbook bilateral-ptosis aetiology.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

patient.chief_complaint: Seven-day progressive bilateral ptosis with complete inability to open eyes, preserved eye movements, no limb weakness, global areflexia.
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. K. is a 33-year-old teacher presenting with a 7-day history of progressive bilateral ptosis. The ptosis began in the left eye and spread to involve the right eye 5 days later. She now has nearly complete bilateral ptosis and cannot open her eyelids voluntarily without using her fingers. She reports mild generalized malaise and fatigue with routine activities over the same period. She denies any diplopia — eye movements are fully intact. She has no difficulty swallowing, speaking, or breathing. She notes no weakness in her arms or legs and was able to walk to the emergency department without difficulty. She has no sensory symptoms. There is no diurnal variation in her ptosis — it does not improve in the morning or worsen with prolonged activity. There is no prior history of similar symptoms. She recalls no recent respiratory illness, gastrointestinal illness, or other viral syndrome preceding the onset. She denies exposure to spoiled food, wounds, or ticks. She takes no medications. The initial concern was myasthenia gravis given the bilateral ptosis, though there is no diurnal variation, extraocular movements are fully preserved, and global areflexia is present on exam.

neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 3.4 L (predicted 3.6 L — 94%). NIF: -48 cmH2O. No diurnal variation in ptosis. Ptosis progressed from left eye to bilateral over 5 days. No fatigability on sustained upgaze. No preceding illness recalled by patient.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact. Heel-shin intact. No ataxia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis — complete inability to open eyelids voluntarily without assistance. On attempted upward gaze, minimal voluntary lid elevation. Pupils equal, round, reactive bilaterally. Extraocular movements FULL in all directions — NO ophthalmoplegia. No diplopia. Bell's phenomenon preserved. No facial weakness. No dysarthria. Gag preserved.
neurological_exam.motor: Upper extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally. Lower extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally. Normal bulk and tone throughout.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Global areflexia — absent biceps, brachioradialis, triceps, patellar, Achilles bilaterally. Plantars downgoing.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact light touch, pinprick, vibration, proprioception in all extremities.
